instructions:
A PDF was filed by hand. Open the file at `attachments.pdf_path` and read it, then produce a structured summary.

Read it as a document, not as text: look at the figures, tables and plots. A result table usually settles what the paper actually achieved faster than the prose does, and a figure often carries the method. If the document is long, read the abstract, introduction, method and results sections in full and skim the rest.

`bibliography` must come from the document itself — its title page, header or footer. The filename is not evidence; it is whatever the person who saved the file happened to type.

`topics` is your judgement. These are the topics this archive tracks; list the slugs this paper genuinely belongs to, and leave the list empty rather than forcing a fit:
- reasoning-evaluation: Reasoning Evaluation — Benchmarks for reasoning and the methodology behind them: what each one actually tests, how contamination and memorization inflate a score, and where a reported gain fails to reproduce. The question the archive answers is which numbers a claim about reasoning can be built on.
- reasoning-faithfulness: Reasoning Faithfulness — The gap between a model's stated chain of thought and the computation that produced its answer: unfaithful or post-hoc rationalization, reasoning that is latent rather than written, encoded or steganographic traces, and what a monitor reading the trace can and cannot catch. The question the archive answers is when a visible reasoning trace is evidence about the model, and when it is only text.
- reasoning-training: Reasoning Training — How a language model acquires long-form reasoning: reinforcement learning against verifiable rewards, process versus outcome supervision, distillation of reasoning traces, and self-training. The question the archive answers is which training signal produces reasoning that generalizes, and what each one costs.
- test-time-scaling: Test-Time Scaling — What a model gains by thinking longer at inference: sampling and verification, search over reasoning steps, self-correction, and the length of the chain itself as a compute knob. The question the archive answers is how accuracy trades against tokens spent, and where that curve flattens.

`relevance` must have one entry per slug you listed in `topics`.

Rules:
- Write in en.
- Ground every statement in the supplied material. If something is not stated,
  leave the field empty rather than inferring it.
- No marketing language. Prefer the specific number over the adjective.
- Return one JSON object matching the schema exactly. No prose around it.

bibliography.abstract: string - the paper's own abstract, verbatim
bibliography.arxiv_id: string - arXiv id if printed on the document, else empty
authors: string - author name, in the order printed
bibliography.doi: string - DOI if printed on the document, else empty
bibliography.title: string - the paper's own title, exactly as printed
bibliography.venue: string - journal, conference or 'preprint'; empty if unclear
bibliography.year: integer - publication year, 0 if the document does not say

concepts: string - reusable ideas this paper relies on or introduces
datasets: string - datasets, benchmarks, corpora or simulators used
output_schema.limitations: string - stated limits plus any the reader should notice
output_schema.method: string - how it works, enough for a reader to explain it
methods: string - named methods, architectures or algorithms
output_schema.one_liner: string - what the paper does, in one sentence, no hype
output_schema.problem: string - the problem it addresses and why it is open

relevance.<topic-slug>: string - why this matters for that specific topic

output_schema.results: string - headline numbers, on which benchmarks, against what
topics: string - slug of a tracked topic this paper belongs to; omit any that do not genuinely apply

payload.title: Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty

bibliography.abstract: LLMs often exhibit Aha moments such as self-correction after tokens like "Wait," yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Standard LLMs collapse mainly through silent divergence, where trajectories drift from the correct answer yet remain locally coherent, so no explicit error triggers reactive self-correction. We introduce an information-theoretic framework that separates reasoning into procedural advancement and epistemic verbalization, the token-level externalization of uncertainty, and prove that sporadic verbalization restores convergence toward the correct answer even without explicit error triggers. Empirically, a minimal doubt cue recovers failed trajectories, and small-scale SFT suffices to instill or suppress this capability, suggesting that strong reasoning hinges less on an extraordinary inner mechanism than on the linguistic habit of externalizing uncertainty. Our framework recasts reasoning as strategic information allocation under uncertainty, offering a new lens for understanding and advancing LLM reasoning.
bibliography.title: Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty

contributions: A taxonomy separating reactive correction (triggered by an explicit surfaced error) from proactive correction (triggered by internal doubt alone), with counts showing proactive correction is essentially absent in standard LLMs and accounts for 22-35% of self-corrections in reasoning models.

The concept of epistemic verbalization: because autoregressive decoding conditions on emitted tokens and not on internal states, a latent uncertainty variable is informationally inert until it is written down, at which point it becomes conditionable and can drive control actions.

A theoretical result (Proposition 5.3) that sporadic epistemic verbalization suffices for convergence — expected residual entropy about the answer goes to zero regardless of how rarely a procedural error trigger fires — formalizing why doubt helps precisely where reactive correction cannot.

Intervention evidence in both directions: injecting a minimal doubt cue into truncated failed rollouts recovers about 15% of them, while suppressing epistemic verbalization at test time or via self-distillation SFT degrades accuracy sharply.
An account of when reasoning distillation works, tying success to whether epistemic tokens fall inside the student's existing distributional support.
result.limitations: The paper's own: analysis is mainly on mathematical reasoning where correctness is verifiable, with extension to other closed-world tasks and the open-world Bayesian formulation left to future work — and it notes that in tool-augmented or interactive settings external observations could surface latent errors independently, reducing the need for epistemic verbalization, which would bound the framework's scope. The nine epistemic tokens are acknowledged as practical proxies that do not cover the full range of uncertainty expression. Both the reactive/proactive classification and the collapse-mode analysis rely on GPT-5 as an automated judge, introducing annotation noise. A reader should add that AIME24 pass@1 is measured on 30 problems, so the Table 5 entries correspond to very small absolute counts — 13.3 to 6.7 is four problems becoming two — and the LLM rows of the reactive/proactive table are explicitly flagged as small samples with N < 50. The claim that suppression is not merely stylistic rests on models partially routing around the mask, which also means the 10% test-time drop understates the effect of true suppression.
result.method: Reasoning is modelled as self-conditioning: each generated token refines the model's belief over the target answer Y without external evidence, and the objective is minimizing H(Y | s_T), with per-step information gain the drop in that conditional entropy. Two informational channels are distinguished. Procedural information accumulates only when an overt error surfaces along a diverged path (Assumption 5.1), so in silent divergence its expected contribution is near zero. Epistemic verbalization emits a token v_t from which the latent reliability assessment Z_t is recoverable; once v_t is in the context, H(Y | s_{t-1}, v_t) <= H(Y | s_{t-1}), with strict inequality when the token carries real information about Z_t (Assumption 5.2). Self-correction is then treated as a control action that acts on this information rather than as the mechanism itself. Empirically: reasoning collapse is measured by having GPT-5 judge 4,800 generations (600 problems x 8 samples) into five collapse modes; reactive versus proactive corrections are counted by a GPT-5 filter looking for a wrong-path-then-correction-then-correct-answer pattern. The causal test truncates every incorrect rollout at relative positions alpha in {0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 0.9}, resumes generation with or without a short injected phrase, draws four continuations, and reports the fraction of originally incorrect rollouts that reach the correct answer. Five conditions separate re-sampling alone (NONE) from doubt alone, intent-to-revisit, and both, across two phrasings ('Hmm' vs 'Wait'). Nine surface tokens ('wait', 'hmm', 'perhaps', 'maybe', 'actually', 'alternatively', 'seems', 'might', 'check') serve as measurement proxies, chosen by their co-occurrence frequency with epistemic verbalization. Suppression is tested two ways: masking those tokens at inference, and self-distillation SFT on 800 of a model's own correct traces generated under an instruction to proceed without expressing uncertainty, so the fine-tuned variant differs from the base only in the absence of epistemic verbalization.
result.one_liner: Separates reasoning into procedural advancement and 'epistemic verbalization' — the token-level externalization of uncertainty — and shows that emitting doubt is what lets a model recover from silent divergence, that injecting a bare doubt cue recovers failed trajectories, and that 800 SFT examples suffice to install or destroy the habit.
result.problem: Aha moments, reflection, self-correction and tokens like 'Wait' are routinely cited as the mechanism behind strong reasoning, but they are lumped into one phenomenon and their computational role is unestablished; prior work documents when such markers fail to predict correction without explaining why. The paper identifies the gap concretely: the dominant failure mode is silent divergence, where a trajectory drifts from the correct answer while staying locally coherent, so no contradiction ever surfaces. Reactive self-correction has nothing to trigger on in that regime, and existing information-theoretic accounts of CoT treat every token as a procedural step, leaving unexplained how a model recovers from a wrong path without outside help.

relevance.reasoning-faithfulness: This is the strongest kind of evidence this topic can get about a visible trace: a causal intervention in both directions on the same tokens. It argues the trace is not decoration — inserting a doubt token the model did not produce recovers failed trajectories, and removing the habit by fine-tuning on the model's own correct traces halves accuracy — so at least this part of the chain of thought is load-bearing rather than post-hoc narration. The mechanism offered is precise and testable: because decoding conditions on emitted tokens rather than on internal states, latent uncertainty is causally inert until verbalized, which is a concrete reason a trace can carry real information about the computation. The 24.4% precision figure cuts the other way and is equally useful here — most expressed doubt is not tracking a real error, so a monitor reading a trace for 'the model noticed something' would be wrong three times in four. The paper's own framing, that strong reasoning may rest on a learnable linguistic habit rather than an extraordinary inner mechanism, is a direct claim about what a reasoning trace is evidence of.
relevance.reasoning-training: Two results bear on training signal. First, 800 examples are enough to install or destroy the behaviour, which places epistemic verbalization on the habit side of the capability/habit line and suggests a large part of what reasoning-oriented SFT transfers is stylistic conditioning rather than knowledge. Second, the distillation analysis gives a concrete predictor of when a reasoning dataset will help a given student: whether the dataset's epistemic tokens already lie within the student's distributional support. That turns 'distillation sometimes fails' into a measurable pre-check, and it explains failures on models with similar size and initial accuracy that the usual capability framing cannot.

result.results: Reasoning collapse occurs in 50-83% of incorrect responses and rises with problem difficulty. Proactive correction is nearly absent in standard LLMs — at most 35 of 4,800 generations, under 1% — while in reasoning models it is 23.7% of self-corrections for Qwen3-8B, 22.2% for Qwen3-14B, 35.0% for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B and 30.7% for the 32B. Its precision is low: 37.3%, 23.9%, 20.5% and 15.8% respectively, averaging 24.4%, so roughly three of four proactive verbalizations second-guess a chain that was already correct — the paper argues an imprecise signal that fires beats a precise one that never does, because silent divergence gives reactive correction nothing to fire on. Injecting a doubt cue into failed trajectories recovers about 15% of incorrect rollouts; expressing uncertainty alone, without naming what went wrong, is enough, and explicit intent to revisit adds little. Recovery falls as the truncation point moves later, but the no-injection baseline falls fastest, reaching near zero at alpha = 0.9, so the gap widens; 'Wait'-style cues slightly beat 'Hmm'-style ones, and recovery tracks benchmark difficulty (MATH500 > AMC23 > AIME24) consistently across Qwen3-8B-Base and 14B-Base. Suppression at test time costs about 10% on avg@8 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-14B/32B, though the models partly route around the mask with alternative phrasings. Self-distillation SFT with epistemic verbalization suppressed cuts AIME24 pass@1 from 13.3 to 6.7 (Qwen2.5-7B), 16.7 to 3.3 (Qwen3-8B-Base), 16.7 to 10.0 (Qwen3-14B-Base), 50.0 to 30.0 (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B) and 80.0 to 43.3 (32B), despite every training trace containing a correct answer. In the other direction, SFT on LIMO-v2 — 800 examples in which 'Wait' appears 77.1 times per response on average — improves AIME24 pass@1 by up to 2.6x for Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3-8B/14B-Base, but degrades DeepSeek-Math-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Math-7B and Qwen3-1.7B-Base; the split is explained by whether epistemic tokens already fall within the student's support, remaining low-probability and high-entropy in models that benefit and outside the support in those that do not.
